title: How Pepper Spray Works
summary: Josh and Chuck discuss how pepper spray works, prompted by the viral "pepper spray cop" meme after UC Davis Lieutenant John Pike pepper-sprayed seated protesters, and the use of pepper spray at Occupy Wall Street protests. They cover oleoresin capsicum (OC) and capsaicin, how it is made and dispensed (stream, mist, fog, foam), its physiological effects, the Scoville heat scale and hot peppers (ghost pepper, Trinidad scorpion), risks such as allergic reactions and asthma, first aid (soap, oil-vs-water chemistry, medicated wipes), legal considerations, and the difference from tear gas. The episode also includes listener mail about the Air Force One episode and a Christmas shout-out, plus a contest announcement.

segments.title: Opening banter and pepper spray cop meme
segments.summary: The hosts open with jokes about the 'don't tase me bro' meme and discuss the viral pepper spray cop meme inspired by the UC Davis incident involving Lieutenant John Pike, including online backlash and his personal information being posted.

segments.title: Why pepper spray works and its controversial use
segments.summary: The hosts explain that pepper spray bypasses pain sensation, causing a physical incapacitation response, and that its use against peaceful, seated protesters, including at Occupy Wall Street, is controversial. Megan Kelly's 'food product' remark is discussed.

segments.title: Oleoresin capsicum, capsaicin, and how pepper spray is made
segments.summary: Pepper spray's active ingredient is oleoresin capsicum (OC), a natural pepper oil containing capsaicin, which is colorless, odorless, and flavorless yet causes blistering at very small amounts. Pepper spray mixes capsaicin with a solvent and propellant in a pressurized canister.

segments.title: Spray patterns: stream, mist, fog, and foam
segments.summary: The hosts describe the stream, mist, fog, and foam spray patterns and their tradeoffs in range, targeting, and wind blowback. They joke about police misusing fog spray.

segments.title: Hot peppers history and the Scoville scale
segments.summary: The hosts discuss historical uses of hot peppers as defense, including Japanese geisha and Maya smoke tactics, and modern very hot peppers like the ghost pepper (bhut jolokia), Trinidad scorpion Butch T, and a ghost-pepper burger at Chunky Burger. They explain the Scoville heat units scale, its origin with Wilbur Scoville's dilution test, and modern HPLC testing, with pepper spray rated roughly 500,000 to 5 million units.

segments.title: Effects of pepper spray and health risks
segments.summary: Pepper spray causes burning in the face, eyes, nose, mouth, and throat lasting about 45 minutes to an hour, with eye swelling and temporary blindness. The hosts discuss the risk of anaphylaxis and asthma complications, and cite an ACLU study in California finding one death in about 600 sprays.

segments.title: First aid for pepper spray exposure and laws
segments.summary: The hosts explain why oil and water don't mix, so water is ineffective on oily capsaicin, and recommend blinking, rinsing with soap such as Dawn dish soap, and medicated wipes. They note that pepper spray laws vary by country and state, including Canada, Belgium, and Hong Kong, and that canisters should be replaced about every three years.

segments.title: Contest announcement
segments.summary: The hosts promote a contest offering a trip to Atlanta, a hotel stay, office tour, lunch, and prizes including a gift card and a Kindle Fire for referrals.

segments.title: Listener mail and Christmas shout-out
segments.summary: The hosts read listener corrections about Air Force One, including that Marine One is a Sikorsky or Black Hawk rather than a Chinook, that the C-17 carries the limos, and an explanation of why Air Force One cannot fly above 40 feet on the ground. They close with a Christmas shout-out to listener Lincoln from his sister Casey.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts thank listeners and give contact information and a sponsor message.
